extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for using (and recognising) free indirect speech / free indirect discourse: how to present a character's thoughts or speech through a third‑person narrator while merging narrator and character voice. Includes linguistic markers, usage notes, distinctions from other modes, examples, and legal/attribution cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merged narrator-and-character voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Free indirect speech is 'a technique of presenting a character's voice partly mediated by the voice of the author', where 'the narrator takes on the speech of the character' and the two voices are merged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use free indirect speech to create the illusion that the character speaks through the narrator; the effect is a blending of authorial/narratorial perspective with the character's subjective voice. This merged voice is the central defining feature and should feel neither fully quoted nor fully reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Free' = roaming viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'free' distinguisher indicates that the author may 'roam from viewpoint to viewpoint' among several different characters rather than being fixed to a single narrator or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may shift focalisation among characters using FID; do so carefully to avoid confusing attribution—signals such as tense, deixis, or a change in lexical register help signal viewpoint changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not announced (no reporting clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free indirect discourse differs from indirect discourse in not announcing what it is doing—omitting explicit reporting verbs or introductory expressions like 'he said' or 'she asked'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop quotation marks and introductory expressions; the subordinate clause carrying the content of reported speech becomes the main clause itself. Antipattern: leaving an ambiguous or stray reporting tag that undermines the 'free' effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater directness than normal indirect speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveys the character's words more directly than normal indirect speech, often reproducing interjections, psycho-ostensive expressions, curses, and swearwords that indirect subordinate clauses normally avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speech-like devices (exclamations, interjections, informal diction) to increase immediacy. Be mindful of register shifts so the voice still reads as the character's rather than as gratuitous authorial flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deictic anchoring to the character
rubrics_metrics.description: When adverbials or deictic pronouns are used in FID, they refer to the coordinates of the character (the speaker/thinker) rather than to those of the external narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure demonstratives, temporal and spatial adverbials, and pronouns reflect the character's perspective (e.g., 'here', 'now', 'that') so the reader experiences the scene from the character's vantage point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person, past-tense with current character perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: FID typically uses linguistic features that indicate a character's current perspective and voice while the narration remains in third-person, past-tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain third-person past as the narrative backbone, but allow momentary shifts into the character's subjective now via diction and syntax without converting to first person or direct quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backshifting of past judgements but not modals
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous judgements, exclamations, opinions, etc., are backshifted in FID (example: 'How differently did every thing now appear...'), whereas modals are not shifted (example: 'She must own that she was tired...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting material into FID, be attentive to tense and mood: shift evaluative past-tense phrasing where appropriate, but retain modal verbs to preserve the character's present sense of obligation/possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exclamatory questions, character-specific locutions, fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: FID frequently employs exclamatory questions, idiosyncratic locutions, syntactical informalities, and sentence fragments to reflect the character's voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce informal or fragmentary syntax to mimic thought processes, but keep coherence so the reader can attribute the voice correctly; overuse can obscure narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology distinction: 'discourse' vs 'style' (spoken vs silent thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Randall Stevenson suggests reserving 'free indirect discourse' for instances where words have actually been spoken aloud, and using 'free indirect style' for cases where the character's silent inward thoughts are being represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose terminology consistently in analysis or teaching: if representing explicit spoken utterances within the narrative, label as FID/discourse; for interior, unspoken thought, consider 'free indirect style'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and summarisation of speech/thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors use FID to provide summaries of conversations or compress a character's speech and thoughts—presenting interior thought with the narrator's economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use FID to condense dialogue or internal monologue for pacing or omniscient commentary. Example: Austen compresses and filters characters' thoughts while preserving vividness; avoid over-compression that erases necessary content or attribution cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to background and minor characters
rubrics_metrics.description: FID can be used for background characters as well as main characters; Austen used indirect speech for background characters in addition to main ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply FID selectively to background figures to enrich perspective or satirise social types. Ensure signals (lexical choices, focalisation markers) are sufficient so readers recognise whose perspective is being filtered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-genre and cross-linguistic use
rubrics_metrics.description: FID appears across literary traditions (German 'erlebte Rede', French 'discours indirect libre', Latin oratio obliqua) and beyond literature (e.g., journalistic retellings, folktales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that conventions and acceptability of FID vary by language and genre; journalists and folklorists may adapt FID differently from novelists. Study genre-specific examples to learn idiomatic usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and attribution risk (blurring authorial responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because FID blurs the boundary between narrator/author and character voice, it can create legal/ethical risks when fictional characters comment on real persons or organisations—attribution may be read as authorial statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fictionalising or portraying real figures, include clear contextual cues attributing opinions to characters if legal risk or defamation is a concern; be cautious that insufficient attribution has been used in court as evidence of authorial intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and stylistic awareness (useful for stylistic effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: FID has historical roots (Goethe, Austen, Flaubert, Kafka, Woolf, etc.) and produces particular stylistic effects—vividness, subjectivity, proximity to character consciousness—valued in modern and realist fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study canonical practitioners to learn idiomatic deployments of FID and to decide what rhetorical or ethical effects you wish to achieve. Emulate techniques (italics, register shifts, focalisation markers) found in successful examples.
